newsitem.title: UK: Asia investment strong but China peaking - UNCTAD.
newsitem.headline: Asia investment strong but China peaking - UNCTAD.

text.p: Asia is still attracting almost two-thirds of total flows into developing countries but foreign direct investment (FDI) into China is likely to peak in 1996, the latest World Investment report from UNCTAD said.

The annual report from the Geneva-based United Nations Conference on Trade and Development said the $65 billion invested in Asia in 1995 was 21 percent up on the previous year. Almost 90 percent of these inflows went to East and Southeast Asia with China alone accounting for $38 billion.
Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand attracted $14 billion last year, compared with $8.6 billion in 1994.
UNCTAD said a key question was whether China, which is second only to the United States as the largest recipient of FDI, could continue to attract such investment.
"After probably a new peak in 1996, FDI inflows may well decline (below $30 billion) temporarily," the report said.

It said government moves towards national treatment policies, more selectivity in screening FDI projects and introduction of measures to prevent speculative investment could reduce the volume of FDI flows. Anti-inflation policies have been another factor.
But the report said China would remain one of the top FDI destinations in the world.
It also noted that Asia was becoming a home base for trans- national corporations (TNCs) which were increasing their FDI flows, with the bulk of these moving in the region itself.

In 1995, FDI outflows in Asia amounted to $43 billion, representing 90 poercent of all developing country outflows. Hong Kong is the single largest outward investor among developing countries, mostly directed at China.

The largest receipients of FDI in Asia in 1995 were China ($37.5 billion), Malaysia ($5.8 billion), Singapore ($5.3 billion), Indonesia ($4.5 billion), Thailand ($2.3 billion) and Hong Kong (2.1 billion).
The largest Asian investors in the region were Hong Kong ($25 billion), Taiwan ($3.8 billion), China ($3.5 billion), Korea ($3.0 billion) and Malaysia ($2.6 billion).
The report also noted a tripling of FDI flows in 1995 into India after liberalisation and deregulation policies and expected this to grow further.

UNCTAD said European companies had been "relatively slow to make direct investments in Asia" but perceived "a changing course" after support from the European Commission and the recently-launched Asia-Europe Investment Promotion Action Plan.
Asia's own biggest companies are heavily engaged in intra-regional investment, accounting for 40 percent of total FDI stock in east and south east Asia.
In 1994, 21 of the top 25 TNCs from developing countries, ranked by foreign assets, were based in Asia.
"Daewoo (Korea) for example is the largest foreign investor in Vietnam and Acer (Taiwan) is the largest investor in Subic bay, the Philippine's largest industrial zone," the report said.

The 10 largest TNCs from developing Asia ranked by foreign assets, in 1994 were: Daewoo (Korea), Hutchinson Whampoa (Hong Kong), Jardine Matheson Holdings (Hong Kong), China State Construction Engineering Corporation (China), China Chemicals Imports and Exports, Samsung Co Ltd (Korea), LG Group (Korea), Hyundai (Korea), Keppel Corporation (Singapore) and San Miguel (Philippines).
